title: New Zealand is determined not to keep China’s espionage a secret
gist: New Zealand's 2026 NZSIS threat assessment names China by name as the only state conducting espionage against NZ 'at scale' — a notably blunter stance than Australia's equivalent assessment — as Beijing retaliates with MP travel bans and diplomatic pressure, while the report also flags Chinese and Russian attempts to embed infrastructure and acquire dual-use or sanctioned technology through NZ.

insights.claim: New Zealand's latest annual NZSIS threat assessment states that while several states conduct espionage against New Zealand, the People's Republic of China is the only country detected doing so 'at scale,' and China's efforts to gain information 'cannot be described as benign.'
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: An explicit, officially named escalation in NZ's public China threat characterization — signals a harder NZ-China security posture that could affect NZ-China trade and diplomatic relations.
insights.quote: There are several states that conduct espionage against New Zealand, but the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the only country we have detected doing it at scale.

insights.claim: New Zealand has long been considered the weakest link in the Five Eyes alliance and the easiest target for China to pressure, but has now named China so consistently in its intelligence warnings that officials joke it has become tougher on Beijing than Australia is.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: A notable reversal in relative Five Eyes toughness — NZ overtaking Australia in explicit China-naming signals a genuine shift in NZ's risk tolerance toward Beijing.
insights.locator: New Zealand had long been considered the weakest link

insights.claim: Mike Burgess, head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, does not name China explicitly in his equivalent threat assessments, unlike New Zealand's NZSIS.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: A direct comparative data point on differing Five Eyes public-attribution strategies toward China — a benchmark for gauging relative diplomatic risk tolerance across partners.
insights.locator: Mike Burgess, the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation

insights.claim: China angrily denounced New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters for describing China as a nation of liars, and the previous month placed travel bans on four backbench NZ MPs who had travelled to Taiwan, in an apparent attempt to set a new red line.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: Concrete retaliatory actions — travel bans on MPs — show Beijing escalating pressure tactics against NZ politicians over Taiwan visits, a preview of how China may respond to other Five Eyes members' Taiwan engagement.
insights.locator: The growing tensions were most evident

insights.claim: NZSIS director-general Andrew Hampton said New Zealand's high global interconnection combined with its Pacific location and proximity to Antarctica make the country 'not only geopolitically relevant, but also attractive to threat actors.'
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: Frames NZ's Antarctic and Pacific geography as an independent driver of espionage targeting beyond Five Eyes membership alone — relevant to NZ's future security-spending trajectory.
insights.quote: These factors in combination make New Zealand not only geopolitically relevant, but also attractive to threat actors.

insights.claim: New Zealand joined other Five Eyes partners in warning that China is targeting their citizens on job sites through an 'aggressive' online recruitment strategy aimed at accessing classified or sensitive information, with national security clearance holders and military personnel particularly at risk.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: A specific, actionable espionage vector — fake job-site recruitment — now flagged across Five Eyes, relevant to corporate and government personnel-risk screening.

insights.claim: NZSIS warned that dual-use technologies with both civilian and military functions are increasingly targeted, noting the distinction has blurred as modern warfare weaponises commercial tools such as AI and off-the-shelf drones.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: Signals expanded regulatory and export-control scrutiny risk for commercial AI and drone technology suppliers connected to New Zealand and similar Five Eyes jurisdictions.
insights.quote: Dual-use technologies have both civilian and military functions, but the distinction has become increasingly blurred with modern warfare now weaponising commercial tools such as AI and off-the-shelf drones.

insights.claim: Purple Mountain Observatory, linked to a Chinese state research institution, had tried to install ground-based space infrastructure in New Zealand, a notable case in the country's growing space sector.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: A concrete named case of Chinese state-linked entities attempting to embed infrastructure in NZ's space sector — relevant to due-diligence screening for foreign investment in NZ space and tech assets.

insights.claim: In one case study in the report, a Russian state-owned organisation sought to acquire specialised components — usable to enhance Russia's military capability and prohibited under sanctions — from the offshore subsidiary of a New Zealand-registered company.
insights.speaker: Anna Fifield
insights.so_what: Demonstrates sanctions-evasion attempts routing through NZ-registered corporate structures — a concrete compliance-risk case for firms with NZ subsidiaries dealing with Russian-linked entities.
insights.locator: In one case study included in the report
